diagnostic_value: Commonest Roman wine amphora in the Indian Ocean. Shape is easy to spot from handle or base; source needs fabric analysis, so a bare "Dressel 2-4" attribution does not tell you which end of the Mediterranean it came from.
Ancestor of the Dressel 2-4. Fabric overlaps with western Dr2-4 and other eastern fabrics; stamps and typology carry the identification.
Early Roman eastern Mediterranean wine container.
Early Italian type; an early date marker.
One of the three Roman staples; signals provisioning rather than luxury exchange.
Globular Spanish oil amphora; a staple container.
Egyptian product; at a Red Sea port it means local supply rather than long-haul import.
Late antique marker. Its presence puts a site in the 5th-7th c. rather than the Periplus horizon.
Late antique marker.
Late antique marker.
Red Sea regional product; signals intra-Red Sea traffic.
Tightly dated Roman fine ware and the single best chronological peg for the Periplus horizon in India. Post-dates Rouletted Ware's first appearance, so ITS without RW is unusual.
Traded as objects rather than for contents; export rationale must be argued case by case.

Long misread as Roman. Indian origin now accepted (Begley 1988). Dating is contested: widest bracket 400 BC-AD 300; commonly 2c BC-1c AD; Schenk argues production ceased in the 1c BC. Schenk reads its distribution as gift exchange tied to Buddhism, not Indo-Roman trade, so RW alone is weak evidence for a Roman-facing port.
Also once misread as Roman because of the red slip. Characteristic form is the sprinkler. Identifiable from publication alone, so older reports can be corrected without re-examining sherds.
Wheeler Types 24 (handi), 25 (casserole), 28-9 (flanged casserole/lid), 4-6 (plain rim dish). Frequently sooted, so used for cooking. Petrography shows several production centres.

THE key provenance link. Internal bamboo-tool wiping from the North Kerala "scooping" technique matched Red Sea finds to Pattanam in 2003, establishing a direct Kerala-Egypt connection. The most location-diagnostic ware in the corpus for the Malabar ports.
Thick-walled handmade black fabric, light in weight, frequently sooted. Found in small numbers throughout the Indian Ocean.
East-coast source; helps distinguish embarkation point from the Malabar wares.
Handle-less conical jar, Indian not Roman despite older literature. Over 50 set into the ground at Kanchipuram. Not yet found outside India.
Pre-Roman horizon. Fabric similarity to RW supported the argument for RW's Indian origin.

vessel_function: liquid storage; water or Arabian wine
diagnostic_value: High-footed calcareous jars with organic temper, lined with bitumen or beeswax, plaster seal at the mouth. The one South Arabian ware with quantitatively significant distribution outside the region.
Basaltic fabric matched to Aden's geology. Identification is explicitly tentative.

Handle-less barrel-shaped jar with bitumen lining. Many Indian sherds once called Roman are actually these. NOT positively identified on Red Sea sites, so its presence points to Gulf rather than Red Sea traffic, and mostly to the Sasanian period (AD 224-651). Possibly the Persian wine of PME 36.
Turquoise alkaline glaze. Production spans a very long period, so undiagnostic for date unless shape or decoration is present.
Distinctive decorated repertoire, confirmed against thin sections from Aksum itself.
Calcareous granitic-tempered fabric with incised bosses; form-plus-fabric combination not known at Aksum. Geologically placed north of Adulis, so a regional marker for the Eritrean coast.
Catch-all for reports that say "Roman amphora" without a type. Retained because excluding it would silently drop most older Indian reports, but it cannot be sourced or closely dated.
Catch-all. Tomber's central warning applies: much pottery called Roman in Indian reports is actually Mesopotamian (Torpedo) or Indian (RW, RPW). Treat every unverified attribution as provisional.

After pottery the most-cited class. Hoards cluster inland in South India, so coins track bullion flow and hoarding behaviour rather than harbour location. Denomination and date matter: Julio-Claudian aurei and denarii differ in meaning from later bronze.
Traded as objects. Sourcing is harder than for pottery; Egyptian and Levantine origins both possible.
Indo-Pacific beads were made in South India and Sri Lanka and exported widely. Direction of travel must be argued per type.
Personal possessions rather than trade goods; presence suggests resident Romans rather than exchange volume.
Small numbers; often a personal item.

Over 95% of all archaeological pepper comes from Egypt's Eastern Desert, so its distribution maps preservation, not trade. Sourced tightly to Malabar, which makes it the strongest organic link to the Kerala ports.
Native to both Yemen and Somalia; cannot discriminate between the two coasts.
Reused Indian ship timber at Red Sea sites is direct evidence of vessels arriving from India rather than of cargo.

Catch-all for reports naming "terra sigillata" without distinguishing Italian from Eastern. Tomber notes the Arikamedu material was reassessed as a mix of ITS, ESA and ESB spanning c. 10 BC-AD 50, so an undifferentiated attribution conceals real chronological range.

Not an import and not diagnostic of contact. Recorded because it is the denominator: at Pattanam 3.54 million local sherds against 6,029 Roman amphora sherds. Without it, imported-ware totals cannot be read as proportions.
